title: Who were the Buffalo Soldiers?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history of the Buffalo Soldiers, the all-Black U.S. Army regiments formed after the Civil War (officially authorized by Congress in 1866) and disbanded with final desegregation in 1951. They cover the origin of the name and its competing explanations, the post-Civil War context that led to the regiments, the Battle of New Orleans and broken promises of freedom, early service in the Indian Wars and frontier duty, West Point graduates such as Henry Flipper, the Spanish American War fights at San Juan Hill under John "Blackjack" Pershing, World War One and Two service, their role in paving the way for desegregation, their work as early national park protectors and trail builders, violence against Black veterans, and the closing administrative details and listener thank-yous.
topics: Black soldiers in the US Army
Stuff You Should Know administrative details

segments.title: Opening banter and Buffalo Soldier song
segments.summary: The hosts open with off-topic banter about Predator and Carl Weathers, then discuss the Bob Marley song Buffalo Soldier and its lyrics, and introduce the topic of the all-Black regiments.

segments.title: Post-Civil War origins of the regiments
segments.summary: The hosts explain that Buffalo Soldiers were all-Black U.S. regiments and soldiers, starting after the Civil War and ending with desegregation around 1951. They note earlier Black enlistees in the Revolutionary War, the postwar surplus of Black veterans, and Congress's 1866 decision to form all-Black peacetime regiments.

segments.title: Battle of New Orleans and broken promises
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Black Phalanx at the Battle of New Orleans, enslaved men recruited by Andrew Jackson with promises of freedom that were not kept, and the army's consolidation of regiments under William T. Sherman.

segments.title: Origin of the name Buffalo Soldiers
segments.summary: The hosts discuss competing explanations for the name: a Native American honor name, and a comparison of Black soldiers' hair to bison wool. They note that the name was given by others, that evidence is uncertain, and that the troops embraced it over time, with a bison patch appearing around 1911.
topics: Smithsonian National Museum of African American History

segments.title: Frontier service and West Point graduates
segments.summary: The regiments were sent west to Kansas, Texas, and New Mexico, often under white officers. The hosts describe Henry Flipper, the first Black West Point graduate in 1877, who was dismissed after a court martial that he maintained was a setup, and his later posthumous pardon by Bill Clinton. They also mention John Hanks and Charles Young.

segments.title: Supply problems and Indian Wars
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the regiments' chronic undersupply on the frontier, the weak state of the post-Civil War army, and the regiments' duties protecting railroad workers, mail carriers, and cattle drives while fighting in the Indian Wars. They discuss the nuance of Native American resistance and massacres on both sides, and the end of the Indian Wars by the 1890s.

segments.title: Spanish American War and San Juan Hill
segments.summary: The Buffalo Soldiers' Tenth Cavalry fought at San Juan Hill in Cuba and the Battle for San Juan in Puerto Rico under John Pershing. Historians say the Black regiments won the battle, while Teddy Roosevelt claimed credit. The hosts describe the event's cultural impact and Pershing's later treatment of Black soldiers in World War One.

segments.title: World War service, desegregation, and legacy
segments.summary: In World War Two Buffalo Soldier units mostly served in support roles, with some combat. The hosts argue their service laid groundwork for military desegregation, with the last all-Black regiment disbanded in 1951, and link this to Brown v. Board of Education. They note Korean War all-Black units and the continued violence against Black veterans.

segments.title: National parks, final Buffalo Soldier, and closing thoughts
segments.summary: The hosts describe Buffalo Soldiers serving as early national park rangers and building trails and cabins in Sequoia and Yosemite from about 1899 to 1913, and note Mark Matthews, the last original Buffalo Soldier, who died in 2005 at 111. They close with the number of Medals of Honor and a suggestion to hear from current service members and Native American listeners.

segments.title: Administrative details and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts read thank-you notes for gifts and mail, including cheese, soap, coasters, and coffee, and sign off with contact information.
